title: Hubble Spies a Scintillating Globular Cluster
caption: The globular cluster NGC 6540, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Stars pack this Hubble view of NGC 6540, a globular cluster in Sagittarius. The brightest wear prominent cross-shaped diffraction spikes. These are imaging artifacts. As starlight passes into the telescope, the hardware inside nudges it slightly, so bright objects gain spikes of light.

A globular cluster is a stable, tightly bound group of stars, from tens of thousands to millions, held close by their mutual gravity. The image combines two Hubble cameras, Wide Field Camera 3 and the Advanced Camera for Surveys. Their fields of view differ slightly, so the picture shows only the patch of sky both captured.

Hubble looked into the cluster's heart as part of an effort to gauge the ages, shapes and structures of the globular clusters near our galaxy's center. Gas and dust there block some of their light and subtly change the colors of their stars. Because these clusters hold clues to our galaxy's earliest history, studying them helps trace how it evolved.

understand.summary: The image combines visible data from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys with near-infrared data from Wide Field Camera 3. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye and passes through dust more readily. The spikes on bright stars come from the telescope itself.
